chunks: And with this chain of narrators, he said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Sometimes Hajj escapes me, so I will perform 'Arfah (pilgrimage ritual) at the grave of Husain (peace be upon him). He said: You have done well, O Bashir! Whoever of the believers visits the grave of Husain (peace be upon him), knowing his right, on a day other than Eid, it is written for him twenty accepted Hajjs, twenty accepted Umrahs, and twenty battles alongside a Messenger Prophet or a just Imam.
And whoever visits him on the day of Eid, it is written for him one hundred Hajjs, one hundred Umrahs, and one hundred battles alongside a Messenger Prophet or a just Imam.

And whoever visits him on the Day of Arafah, knowing his right, it is written for him one thousand accepted Hajjs, one thousand accepted Umrahs, and one thousand battles alongside a Messenger Prophet or a just Imam.
He said, so I said to him: And how can I have the reward of the standing (at Arafah)?

He said, so he looked at me as if slightly angry, then said: O Bashir! Indeed, when the believer visits the grave of Husain (peace be upon him) on the Day of Arafah, and performs ritual bath in the Euphrates, then turns towards it, it is written for him for every step a Hajj with its rituals, and I do not know him except that he said: and an Umrah and a battle.
ai.seo_question: What are the rewards for visiting Imam Husain's grave on the Day of Arafah?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq highlights the unique status of Karbala as a spiritual substitute for Mecca, where the physical act of Ziyarah compensates for missed Hajj obligations through multiplied rewards. The specific emphasis on bathing in the Euphrates (Al-Furat) on the Day of Arafah underscores the geographical and ritualistic connection between the martyrdom site and the Prophet’s final sermon, elevating the visitor’s standing to that of a companion of the Infallibles. This tradition reflects the Shia theological view that devotion to Ahl al-Bayt is intrinsically linked to the acceptance of worship.
